intro: When you search for a leasehold conveyancer near you, you're likely buying or selling a flat or a leasehold house and need someone who understands the extra layers that come with leasehold property. A local conveyancer can look at the lease, service charges and management information, and explain what these mean for your move. We introduce you to a suitable UK conveyancer who will quote you directly, with fees on application.
need_heading: What people searching for a leasehold conveyancer usually need
need_lead: Leasehold transactions bring their own set of checks and potential delays, so you need a conveyancer who deals with them routinely.
needs: You are buying a flat and want the lease looked at carefully before you commit, especially the length remaining and any restrictions it contains.
You are selling a leasehold property and need someone to obtain and explain the management pack from the freeholder or managing agent.
You are remortgaging a flat and your lender requires a conveyancer to check the lease and service charge arrangements.
You have spotted high service charges or planned major works and need advice on what they mean for your purchase or sale.
You want a conveyancer who is familiar with the area and can deal with local managing agents and freeholders efficiently.
context_heading: What to understand about leasehold conveyancing
context: Leasehold conveyancing involves checking the lease itself, including how many years are left, what the ground rent is and how service charges are calculated and demanded. Your conveyancer will also raise enquiries with the freeholder or managing agent, often through a management pack, which can take time to arrive and may need follow-up questions.

Conveyancing in England and Wales can only be carried out by solicitors regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority or by licensed conveyancers regulated by the Council for Licensed Conveyancers. Both must hold professional indemnity insurance and follow strict rules on handling client money. Many lenders also require your conveyancer to be on their approved panel, so it is worth checking this early.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Whether you are buying, selling or remortgaging the leasehold property, and the property type.
The approximate length of the lease remaining, if you know it.
Whether there are any known issues with service charges, ground rent or major works.
The name of the freeholder or managing agent, if you have it.
Your lender's name if you are buying with a mortgage, so panel membership can be checked.
Your preferred location or area, since you searched for a conveyancer near you.
questions: How do you handle leasehold transactions and what do you charge for looking at the lease and management pack?
Are you on my lender's panel, or will you need to instruct another firm?
What is your experience with the freeholder or managing agent for this property?
How will you keep me informed about delays with the management pack?
What are the key things I should be aware of in the lease, such as the length remaining or ground rent terms?
Do you charge extra for dealing with major works or service charge disputes?

faqs.q: Why do I need a leasehold conveyancer rather than a general one?
faqs.a: Leasehold property involves additional documents such as the lease, service charge accounts and management packs. A conveyancer who deals with these regularly will be better placed to spot issues and explain them to you.

faqs.q: How long does leasehold conveyancing take?
faqs.a: It varies with the complexity of the lease and how quickly the management pack is provided. Your conveyancer can give you an idea once they have the information.

faqs.q: What is a management pack and why does it matter?
faqs.a: It is a package of information from the freeholder or managing agent covering service charges, planned works and building insurance. Your conveyancer needs it to answer questions about the lease and the building.

faqs.q: Can iComply recommend a specific conveyancer near me?
faqs.a: We introduce you to a suitable UK conveyancer based on your needs, but we do not recommend or endorse any particular firm. You should satisfy yourself that the conveyancer is right for you.
